title: All Souls (2 November)
hook: many churches remember all the faithful departed, and families visit graves

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Saints, every saint, known and unknown. Your line was for all the saints. Whose name did you say out loud? Day one thousand fifty-six.

Dusk in a cemetery. A woman kneels and pulls weeds from around a stone, then wipes the name with her sleeve. Her son sets a candle in a red glass jar at the foot of the grave and shields the match from the wind. Across the rows, other little flames come on, one by one, until the whole hillside flickers. Someone has brought flowers. Someone has brought a thermos. Nobody is in a hurry. In some countries, this is what the second day of November looks like. Yesterday the church remembered the saints. Today it remembers everyone else who has died in faith. Today, All Souls.
screen: `A CANDLE IN A RED GLASS JAR.`

segments.voice: All Saints and All Souls sit side by side on purpose. One day for the cloud of witnesses. The next for the faithful departed: grandparents, friends, a child, the people whose graves we know. Grief comes first. At the tomb of his friend Lazarus, in John's Gospel, the King James Bible says it in two words: "Jesus wept." He knows what he's about to do, and he weeps anyway. In the story, grief isn't a lack of faith. And earlier in the same chapter, the hope: "I am the resurrection, and the life." Paul holds both together when he writes to the church in Thessalonica about those who have died. He doesn't tell them not to grieve. He tells them "that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." Sorrow, yes. But sorrow with hope in it. Churches keep this day in different ways. Catholics pray for the dead, trusting that God's mercy can still be at work in them, purifying them, and on this day Masses are offered for all the faithful departed. Orthodox Christians pray for the departed too, in memorial services held through the year. Protestant churches differ. Some don't pray for the dead and instead give thanks for their lives and entrust them to God; some, including some Anglicans, keep All Souls with prayers. In some places, families go to the graves, clean them, and light candles. The carry comes from an old prayer of the Western church, which asks God to give the dead eternal rest, and to let perpetual light shine on them. In Latin it begins with the word requiem, rest. That's why a Mass for the dead is called a requiem. Rest, and light. Two gifts asked for those we can't hold anymore.

Here's the practice: light a candle for someone who has died. If you can, light a real one now, safely, or switch on a small lamp. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who has died. Say their name. Let one ordinary memory come: their laugh, their hands, a phrase they always used. Let whatever you feel be there. If you pray, you can use the old words: rest eternal grant unto them, and let light shine on them. If you don't, simply watch the flame, and hold them in it. The bell holds the time.
All Souls. The day after All Saints, when churches remember all the faithful departed, and families visit graves and light candles.
Your line: rest eternal. Today, say the name of someone who has died to someone who knew them, or visit a grave, or leave the candle burning a little longer. Day one thousand fifty-six.

howItsDone: On All Souls, Catholics and some Anglicans pray for the faithful departed and offer Masses or services for them; in some countries families clean and decorate graves and light candles, and some churches read out the names of those who died in the past year.
